_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 610 words, six questions in text order: detail, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase and a final question linking the ending to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Changing step
subtitle: At sixteen, Mira Collins left a top ballet school to study engineering. Now nineteen, she explains why she has hardly ever looked back.

cards.text: From the age of eleven, my life was organised in counts of eight. I boarded at a specialist dance school in the north of England, where the day began with ballet class at half past eight and ended, if we were lucky, at six. Academic lessons were squeezed into the gaps. I loved it, and I was good at it, although perhaps not quite as good as I needed to be. Everyone there had been the best dancer in their home town. My bedroom wall was covered in posters of famous dancers. At the school, being the best in your town made you completely ordinary.
cards.question: What does the writer say about the other pupils at the school?
choices: They had all been outstanding dancers before they arrived.
They worked less hard than she did.
They found the academic lessons difficult.
Most of them came from the same town.
cards.highlight: Everyone there had been the best dancer in their home town.
cards.why: 'Everyone there had been the best dancer in their home town', which is why being the best was ordinary. Nothing compares how hard they worked.

cards.text: The physics teacher, Mr Okafor, was the only member of staff who seemed unaware that we were supposed to be future stars. He wore the same brown cardigan every day, called everyone 'young scientist' and taught us exactly as if we were going to be scientists, which annoyed most of my classmates. I found myself looking forward to his lessons more than I wanted to admit. One afternoon he explained how a spinning dancer turns faster by pulling in her arms, and wrote the equation on the board. I had done that movement a thousand times. Nobody had ever told me why it worked.
cards.question: What does the writer suggest about the lesson on spinning?
choices: It made her realise she had been turning incorrectly.
It was the first physics lesson she had ever enjoyed.
It helped her understand something familiar in a completely new way.
It persuaded her classmates that physics was useful.
cards.highlight: I had done that movement a thousand times. Nobody had ever told me why it worked.
cards.why: She knew the movement well but 'nobody had ever told me why it worked'. She was already looking forward to his lessons, so it was not the first she enjoyed.

cards.text: The decision itself took about a year, and most of it happened inside my head. I did not tell my parents, who had made real sacrifices to pay for the school, and I certainly did not tell my teachers. When I finally spoke to my ballet teacher, at the end of a rehearsal, she did not react at all for what felt like a full minute. Then she said she had been wondering when I would get round to it. My parents, when I told them that evening, were calmer than I had feared. I still do not know whether her comment was meant as a compliment.
cards.question: What does 'it' refer to in 'when I would get round to it'?
choices: paying back what her parents had spent
telling her teacher she wanted to leave dance
finishing the rehearsal properly
asking for advice about her future
cards.highlight: she said she had been wondering when I would get round to it
cards.why: The teacher had been waiting for Mira to announce 'the decision' to leave. The rehearsal had already ended, so 'it' cannot be finishing it.

cards.text: Moving to an ordinary sixth-form college was a shock in ways I had not expected. Nobody stood up straight, and nobody stretched before climbing the stairs. Lessons started at nine and there was a whole hour for lunch, which I spent the first week not knowing what to do with. In my second term, our physics group entered a competition to build a bridge out of spaghetti that could hold a brick. Ours collapsed spectacularly, but I realised during the planning that I had not thought about dancing for three whole days. That had never happened before.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the spaghetti bridge?
choices: to show how talented her group was at engineering
to explain why she found college lessons too easy
to suggest that she missed the discipline of dance school
to show the moment she noticed how absorbed she was in her new subject
cards.highlight: I realised during the planning that I had not thought about dancing for three whole days
cards.why: The point is that she 'had not thought about dancing for three whole days' for the first time. The bridge 'collapsed spectacularly', so it does not show talent.

cards.text: People often assume I must regret wasting all those years. I don't, and I am getting slightly tired of saying so. Dance taught me to practise something boring until it becomes easy, to fall over in front of people and get up again, and to take criticism without bursting into tears, at least not until I got home. All of that has been more useful at university than anything I learned in a maths class. I am still slower at calculations than most of my course, but I do not panic. My engineering friends groan about failed experiments. To me, a failed experiment feels like an ordinary Tuesday.
cards.question: What does the writer mean when she says a failed experiment 'feels like an ordinary Tuesday'?
choices: It happens to her at the start of most weeks.
It is a normal setback that she is used to dealing with.
It makes her want to give up for the rest of the day.
It is too boring to be worth discussing.
cards.highlight: To me, a failed experiment feels like an ordinary Tuesday.
cards.why: Dance taught her to 'fall over in front of people and get up again', so failure feels routine. The phrase is about how normal it feels, not about a real day of the week.

cards.text: I still dance, though only on Thursday evenings, in a church hall, with a group of retired women who are far more fun than anyone I trained with. This year, for my second-year project, I designed a small device that measures the forces on a dancer's ankle as she lands from a jump. While testing it, I caught myself counting the rhythm under my breath, five, six, seven, eight, just as I did at eleven. The numbers mean something different now, I suppose. But I have never really stopped counting.
cards.question: What is the writer's main point in the final paragraph?
choices: She is planning to return to dancing professionally.
She enjoys her Thursday class more than her studies.
Dance is still part of who she is, even in her new field.
She finds engineering less satisfying than dance.
cards.highlight: But I have never really stopped counting.
cards.why: The counting takes us back to the opening 'counts of eight': dance still shapes her engineering. She dances only for fun, so there is no plan to return professionally.
